result:
Solution 2 is the one I judge most likely correct, because it keeps both the density of cut edges and the logarithmic time scale.

**Cut times.** A cut time requires the edge crossed at time k to be crossed exactly once. The fingers are finite dead ends, so their edges are crossed an even number of times. Only spine edges can therefore give cut times.

**Density of cut edges.** Ignoring finger excursions, the spine walk steps up with probability 1/(1+λ) and down with probability λ/(1+λ). The probability of ever returning from i+1 to i is λ. So spine edge i is crossed exactly once with probability 1−λ. By regeneration at cut levels, the fraction of cut edges among spine edges tends to 1−λ.

**Time scale.** The walk inside a finger of length i is biased toward the tip, with ratio 1/λ. Escaping back to the base takes time of order λ^{−i}. At each spine level there is a constant probability of a deep excursion, so the time T_n to reach level n satisfies (1/n) log T_n → log(1/λ) almost surely. Hence the maximum spine level reached by time N is about log N / log(1/λ).

**Combining.** M(N) ≈ (1−λ) · log N / log(1/λ), so the limit is (1−λ)/(−log λ).

**The other solutions.** Solution 1 treats every closed spine edge as a cut time and so omits the density factor 1−λ. Solution 3 claims the limit of M(N)/N, not M(N)/log N, and answers 0, which does not address the question asked.

CHOICE: 2
